title: What is a savepoint (`SAVEPOINT sp1` → work → `ROLLBACK TO sp1` to undo only the work after the savepoint while keeping the rest of the transaction), and when do you use it (partial retry within a larger transaction, batch processing where one record fails but you don't want to discard the whole batch)?
shortTitle: SQL Savepoints: Partial Rollback Within a Transaction
keyPoints: A savepoint is a named marker inside an open transaction, created with `SAVEPOINT name`.
`ROLLBACK TO name` undoes only the changes made after the savepoint while keeping everything before it intact and the transaction still open.
A full `ROLLBACK` throws away the entire transaction; `ROLLBACK TO savepoint` is surgical partial rollback.
Rolling back to a savepoint invalidates any savepoints created after it, because time has rewound past them.
Use savepoints for batch processing where one bad record should be skipped without discarding the whole batch.
In JDBC, use `Connection.setSavepoint(name)` and `connection.rollback(savepoint)`; in Spring, `Propagation.NESTED` uses savepoints under the hood.

s1_definition.oneliner: A savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction; ROLLBACK TO it undoes only the work after the bookmark, so one bad step does not sink the whole transaction.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Savepoint** – a named marker inside an open transaction, created with `SAVEPOINT name`.
- **Partial rollback** – `ROLLBACK TO name` undoes only the changes made after the savepoint; everything before it stays intact and the transaction remains open.
- **Difference from full ROLLBACK** – a full `ROLLBACK` discards the entire transaction; `ROLLBACK TO savepoint` is surgical.
- **Invalidation** – rolling back to a savepoint invalidates any savepoints created after it.
- **`RELEASE SAVEPOINT`** – discards the savepoint when you no longer need it, freeing resources.
- **Use cases** – batch processing with per-record isolation, and partial retry of a transient failure within a larger transaction.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine processing a batch of a hundred salary credits for National Bank of India inside one transaction. Before each credit you drop a bookmark (savepoint). If crediting employee number 57 fails because their account is frozen, you do not tear up the whole batch – you rewind to the bookmark just before 57 (`ROLLBACK TO sp57`), skip that one, log it, and carry on from 58. The 56 good credits already done stay, and the transaction stays open.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Transaction Timeline with Savepoints:

  BEGIN
    │
    ├── UPDATE emp 1 (credit Rs.10,000)    ← stays
    │
    ├── SAVEPOINT sp2
    │      │
    │      ├── UPDATE emp 2 (credit Rs.10,000)    ← FAILS
    │      │
    │      └── ROLLBACK TO sp2    ← undo only emp 2
    │
    ├── UPDATE emp 3 (credit Rs.10,000)    ← stays
    │
    └── COMMIT
         │
         ▼
    Result: emp 1 and emp 3 credited.
            emp 2 skipped and logged.
            One transaction, partial failure handled.

Full ROLLBACK vs Partial ROLLBACK:
┌────────────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────────────────┐
│ ROLLBACK                   │    │ ROLLBACK TO sp2                │
│ Undoes everything          │    │ Undoes only work after sp2     │
│ Transaction ends           │    │ Transaction stays open         │
│ ┌───┐┌───┐┌───┐           │    │ ┌───┐┌───┐┌───┐               │
│ │ ✗ ││ ✗ ││ ✗ │           │    │ │ ✓ ││ ✗ ││   │ (can continue) │
│ └───┘└───┘└───┘           │    │ └───┘└───┘└───┘               │
└────────────────────────────┘    └────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A savepoint is a named marker you set inside an open transaction. You create it with `SAVEPOINT` followed by a name, do more work, and if that work goes wrong you issue `ROLLBACK TO` that name, which undoes only the changes made after the savepoint while keeping everything before it intact. The transaction stays open. This is surgical, partial rollback – very different from a full `ROLLBACK`, which throws away the entire transaction.

The two situations where savepoints shine are partial retry and batch processing with per-record isolation. For batch processing, you want the efficiency of one transaction but you do not want a single poison record to force the whole batch to roll back. You set a savepoint before each record; when a record fails, you roll back to its savepoint, skip it, and carry on.

In the National Bank of India nightly salary batch, Rajesh credits many employee accounts in one transaction. Occasionally one account is frozen so its credit fails. The service sets a savepoint before each credit; when the frozen account throws, it rolls back to that savepoint, logs the skip, and carries on. At the end it commits once, so every good credit lands atomically and the frozen one is left untouched. In JDBC this maps to `setSavepoint` and `rollback(savepoint)`, and in Spring the `NESTED` propagation uses savepoints under the hood. The caution is that holding a huge transaction with thousands of savepoints keeps locks and undo data alive, so for very large batches prefer chunking into shorter transactions.

Remember one sentence: a savepoint is a bookmark inside a transaction, and rolling back to it undoes only the work after the bookmark, so one bad step never sinks the whole transaction.
